title: Study Map Rules and the Strip Method

cards.prompt: Profiles and permission sets vs. the sharing model: what does each control?
answer: Profiles/permission sets = what you can DO (object CRUD, FLS, apps, tabs, record type access, Apex/Visualforce access, login hours/IPs). Sharing = which RECORDS you can SEE (OWD, role hierarchy, sharing rules, teams, manual sharing).
cards.why: Settles a large share of security questions.
cards.strip: Answer mentions role, sharing, or which records → not a profile answer.

cards.prompt: What is the role of OWD vs. everything else in the sharing model?
answer: OWD is the most restrictive floor. Roles, sharing rules, teams, and manual sharing only OPEN access; they never restrict.
cards.why: To restrict visibility → change OWD. To grant more → sharing rules, roles, teams.
cards.strip: 'Only' / 'restrict' → OWD. 'Give access' → sharing rule, team, or manual share.

cards.prompt: Which direction does the role hierarchy grant access?
answer: Upward only: managers see subordinates' records. Peers at the same level see nothing of each other's under Private OWD; use a sharing rule.

cards.prompt: Which login settings block users and which only verify them?
answer: Profile Login IP Ranges and profile Login Hours BLOCK. Org-wide Trusted IP Ranges only decide whether identity verification is required.
cards.why: Profile = bouncer; org trusted IPs = ID check. Org-wide login hours don't exist.

cards.prompt: When do you use a permission set instead of a profile?
answer: When only SOME users on a profile need extra access. Profile = baseline for a job; permission set = extra access layered on top. Users have one profile, many permission sets; muting in permission set groups removes access.
cards.strip: 'Some users on a profile need X' → permission set.

cards.prompt: Data Import Wizard vs. Data Loader vs. third-party tools: limits and uses?
answer: Import Wizard: up to 50,000; Accounts, Contacts, Leads, Solutions, Campaign Members, custom objects; duplicate matching; no export or delete. Data Loader: all objects, insert/update/upsert/delete/export; 5 million is the recommended threshold, not a hard cap. Third-party: very large volumes. Basic Data Import: Setup toggle giving reps a guided contact/lead CSV import.

cards.why: 'Custom' and 'Standard' are report TYPES (which data), not formats (layout).

cards.prompt: Unique field vs. validation rule vs. matching rule vs. duplicate rule?
answer: Unique field: blocks exact duplicates in one field (case sensitive or insensitive). Validation rule: blocks saves failing a formula ('required IF...'). Matching rule: defines what counts as a duplicate, incl. fuzzy. Duplicate rule: uses a matching rule to alert or block.

cards.prompt: Which field types can be controlling vs. dependent in a field dependency?
answer: Controlling: standard picklist, custom picklist, checkbox. Dependent: custom picklist, custom multi-select picklist. Formula fields: neither.

Lookup: optional, child keeps its own owner and sharing, no roll-ups, child survives parent delete. Master-detail: required, child inherits owner and sharing, roll-up summaries on parent, cascade delete, max 2 per object. Junction object = two master-details for many-to-many.
cards.why: Exam 2 Q23. Master-detail child = dependent; lookup child = roommate.

cards.prompt: What do record types control, and how do they relate to business processes?
answer: Record types control picklist values, page layout assignment (with profile), Lightning page assignment, and business process. One business process can serve many record types; each record type uses one. Record types never control which records users see.
cards.why: Business processes: Sales (Opportunity Stage), Support (Case Status), Lead (Lead Status), Solution (Status).

cards.prompt: When does Flow beat a built-in automation feature?
answer: When the built-in feature covers only PART of the requirements. If the built-in feature covers everything, it wins. Code (Apex) is the last resort.
cards.why: Big Deal Alert (email only) + task needed → Flow. Auto-response with entries covers everything → auto-response. Prospect email + manager alert → auto-response + Flow.
cards.strip: Count the requirements; check each tool against all of them.

cards.prompt: Assignment vs. auto-response vs. escalation rules?
answer: Assignment: who owns it when created (cases, leads). Auto-response: one email to the submitter (cases, leads; no tasks, no CC). Escalation: time-based reassign/notify (cases only). Each: one active rule, many entries, first match wins.

cards.prompt: What actions can an approval process take?
answer: TEFO: Task, Email alert, Field update, Outbound message. Stages: initial submission (locks record), final approval, final rejection, recall.
cards.why: No Apex, no record creation. Exam 1 Q31.

cards.prompt: When should a task go to Agentforce vs. Flow?
answer: Language and judgment (summarizing, drafting) → AI. Strict, deterministic rules and compliance ('without exception') → Flow, which an agent can call as an action. Agentforce has the same access as its user.

cards.prompt: What are the 6 steps of the Strip Method?
answer: 1) Subject: which exact object or feature. 2) Verb: restrict/grant, display/store, block/verify. 3) Defining condition: the detail that rules out the rest. 4) Count the requirements. 5) Strip the traps. 6) Then use Salesforce knowledge.
cards.why: Also check what's MISSING from the question, and WHO is acting (admin vs. user).

cards.prompt: What trap patterns show up in wrong answers?
answer: Absolute words (always, only, any); made-up names (Phone-to-Case, $CHANGED, 'Run All Reports'); wrong object in the name (Web-to-Lead for cases); code when clicks work; too much permission (Modify/View All Data); sharing rules used to restrict; extra overpromising clause; partial solutions; other products (Content Builder); real feature in the wrong place (Default Account Team in 'Administrator Settings').
cards.why: Red flags, not automatic eliminations: real absolutes exist. Specific conditional answers usually describe real behavior.
